title: Lists in .NET and in the engine
sub: Reverse Nodes in k-Group, LinkedList<T> from the inside, and an index-based list with no allocations
cards/0/title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group: the problem
cards/0/body:
Reverse Nodes in k-Group (LeetCode #25, hard). Reverse the list in groups of k nodes; if fewer than k nodes remain at the end, that tail stays as it is. Only links may change, not values; 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 5000. The follow-up: O(1) extra memory.

There is no new technique here: it is the reversal from the lists lesson applied to a piece, plus a dummy node. The difficulty is in the boundaries: where the group ends, what its new head attaches to, and where its new tail will point. The problem is hard not because of the idea but because on a whiteboard it is easy to lose a single link. The interviewer watches how you keep four pointers in your head and check them on an example.
cards/0/code:
// 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
ReverseKGroup(head, 2);   // 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5   (5 is a tail shorter than k)
ReverseKGroup(head, 3);   // 3 → 2 → 1 → 4 → 5   (4 → 5 is left alone)
ReverseKGroup(head, 1);   // unchanged
cards/1/q: The list 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8, k = 3. What does ReverseKGroup return?
cards/1/explain: The two full groups [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] are each reversed in place. The remainder 7 → 8 is shorter than k = 3 and, by the statement, stays as it is.
cards/1/wrong/1: The tail 7 → 8 is shorter than k = 3: by the statement it is not touched, even if it is “almost a group”.
cards/1/wrong/2: That is reversing the whole list. Groups are reversed separately, and the order of the groups does not change.
cards/2/body:
Before the head there is a dummy, and groupPrev is the node before the current group (initially dummy). One iteration:

1. Count k nodes from groupPrev: kth is the last node of the group. Not enough nodes — stop, leave the tail alone.
2. groupNext = kth.next — the first node after the group.
3. Reverse the group with the same prev/cur/next loop, but prev starts at groupNext instead of null. Then the former first node of the group points to the next group right away — the tail is attached by itself.
4. Attach the head: groupPrev.next = kth — the former last node is now first.
5. groupPrev = first — the former first node of the group is now its last and stands before the next group.

Invariant: before each iteration everything up to and including groupPrev is done, and everything after it is untouched. Each node is touched twice (counting and reversing): time O(n), memory O(1).
cards/2/flow/0: kth = groupPrev + k steps (not enough — stop)
cards/3/explain: Counting follows the links: kth = kth.next. The reversal starts with prev = groupNext so that the former first node of the group points to the next group right away. first is remembered before attaching: it is the former head of the group, which has become its tail. groupPrev.next = kth attaches the new head, and groupPrev = first sets the boundary before the next group.
cards/4/task: Step through 1 → … → 8 with k = 3. The rig stops before the second group and before the tail.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The first group is done: 3 → 2 → 1 → 4 → … The second one is [4, 5, 6]. Where will 1.next point once it is reversed and attached?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: 1 is the former first node of the first group, now its tail and groupPrev. Attaching with groupPrev.next = kth points it at 6: the former last node of the second group has become its head. And after the reversal 4 points to 7 — prev started at groupNext.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: 7 → 8 is left, k = 3. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: Counting from groupPrev = 4 hits null on the third step: kth == null, break. By the statement a tail shorter than k is not touched, and 4.next already points to 7 — the reversal of the second group attached it.
cards/5/q: On 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 with k = 2 this code returned 2 → 1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: The reversal starts with prev = null, as for a whole list — and the former first node of the group points nowhere: 1.next = null, and the rest 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 is cut off. The next count from groupPrev = 1 hits null at once, and the loop ends. It must be prev = groupNext.
cards/6/body:
The collections unit covered the essentials: LinkedList<T> is a doubly linked circular list, operations on a node are O(1), search is O(n). Now — how it is built in the dotnet/runtime sources and what follows from that.

Fields. The list has head, count, version and a helper field for serialization; there is no “tail” field. A LinkedListNode<T> node stores list (whose node it is), next, prev and item. The ring: head.prev is the last node, so Last is simply head?.prev, O(1), and AddLast is an insertion before head. The ring is hidden from the outside: Next of the last node and Previous of the first return null.

Whose node. The list field catches mistakes: Remove(node) with a node from another list throws InvalidOperationException, and so does AddFirst(node) with a node that still belongs somewhere. After Remove the node is detached (list, next, prev are cleared), and it can be inserted again with no new allocation. The new LinkedListNode<T>(value) constructor is public: nodes can be prepared in advance and kept in a pool.

Version. Every change increments version; the enumerator is a struct, and if the list is modified in the middle of a foreach, the next MoveNext throws InvalidOperationException. Count is stored — O(1); Contains and Find walk the ring with EqualityComparer<T>.Default — O(n). There is no indexer.

Node size on 64 bits: a 16-byte object header, three 8-byte references and the value — 44 for an int, 48 bytes with alignment, for 4 bytes of data.
cards/6/deep:
Why a ring rather than head and tail. One head field instead of two: Last = head.prev, and inserting at the front and at the back is the same operation, “insert before head”, except that in the first case head then moves to the new node. Fewer branches, fewer empty-list special cases. The price is that Next and Previous have to compare with list.head to hide the ring, so every node needs a reference to its list.

Then and now. In .NET Framework (since 2.0) the list is built the same way: a ring, a single head field and the same four node fields — so a node costs the same. The struct enumerator does not allocate in a foreach over a variable of type LinkedList<T>; casting to IEnumerable<T> boxes it — the same trap as with List<T>.

In Unity the object header on 64 bits is also 16 bytes — in both Mono and IL2CPP (a class pointer and a monitor field), so the order of the cost is the same: tens of bytes and an allocation per element. During a collection the Boehm GC visits every node, and the non-moving heap never gathers them back into a dense block.
cards/7/q: Which statements about LinkedList<T> are true? Select all.
cards/7/options/0: list.Last is O(1): it is head.prev in the ring
cards/7/options/1: list.Remove(node), where node is from another list, throws InvalidOperationException
cards/7/options/2: A removed node can be inserted again with AddFirst(node) and no new allocation
cards/7/options/3: LinkedList<T> has an O(1) indexer list[i]
cards/7/options/4: list.Last.Next returns list.First, because the list is circular
cards/7/explain: There is no tail field, but the tail is always head.prev — O(1). The node’s list field lets the list check that the node is its own, and a foreign one is rejected with an exception. After Remove the node is detached, and AddFirst(node) inserts the same object. There is no indexer at all — only a walk. The ring is internal: Next of the last node returns null.
cards/8/title: Why you almost never need a linked list
cards/8/body:
“I’ll use a LinkedList — insertion is O(1)” is a common interview mistake. It is O(1) only when you already hold the node. Finding the place to insert is an O(n) walk, and walking nodes is slower than walking an array: each hop is a load from an arbitrary memory location and often a cache miss. List<T>.Insert in the middle is O(n) too, but it shifts a contiguous block with one memory copy — on thousands of elements that is often faster than getting to the spot through links.

Unity adds the garbage collector to this: every AddLast(value) is a new heap object, and the Boehm GC does not compact the heap, so the nodes stay scattered and every collection visits all of them.

When a list fits: you need order and O(1) removal or moving of a known node, with the nodes stored elsewhere — in a dictionary, for example. That is how an LRU cache works (the data-structure design unit). When it does not: order does not matter — List<T> and O(1) removal by swapping with the last element (the in-place arrays unit); you need a queue or a stack — Queue<T> and Stack<T>; you need a deque — a ring buffer.
cards/9/q: Unity, up to 2000 projectiles in flight. Every frame some hit and are removed, new ones are added; iteration order does not matter. What do you use?
cards/9/options/0: List<Projectile> and removal by swapping with the last element
cards/9/options/2: Dictionary<int, Projectile> keyed by projectile id
cards/9/explain: Order does not matter, so remove by swapping with the last element: O(1), nothing shifts, the array is reused, and after warm-up there are no allocations. It is convenient to remove while iterating from the end, so the element moved into place has already been checked.
cards/9/wrong/1: Removal by node is O(1), but every new projectile is a new heap node — garbage every frame — and iteration jumps around memory. Swapping with the last is O(1) too, with no allocations.
cards/9/wrong/2: A dictionary is needed if projectiles are looked up by id. Here they are only iterated, iterating a dictionary is slower than an array, and enumeration order is not guaranteed.
cards/10/title: A list on indices in an array
cards/10/body:
Nodes do not have to be objects. A list can live in an array of structs struct Node { int value; int next; }: a “reference” is an index, “null” is −1. Freed cells are gathered into a free list through the same next field: allocating a node pops the head of the free list, freeing one pushes it back. Both operations are O(1).

What this buys you. Zero allocations once the array has grown to its working size. The nodes sit in one contiguous block — iteration is cache-friendly. An array of structs without references is unmanaged: you can put it in a NativeArray<Node> and walk it in a Burst job, where classes are not allowed. Indices survive array growth and are saved as plain numbers, while Unity’s serializer stores class fields by value by default: a graph of references between node objects does not get through it without [SerializeReference].

That is also how Dictionary works in .NET: bucket chains are next indices in the entries array, and removed entries are linked into a free list. Every technique in this unit carries over to indices one to one: cur.next becomes next[cur], and null becomes −1.
cards/10/deep:
Stale indices. If someone outside holds a node’s index, and the node is freed and its cell handed out again, the index silently points at someone else’s data. The cure is a generation: the cell keeps a version counter that grows on every free, and the external handle is a pair (index, version); a version mismatch means the handle is stale. That is exactly how Entity in Unity Entities works: Index and Version, with free entity indices reused.

In Burst. A NativeArray<Node> with Allocator.Persistent lives across frames, an IJob takes it as a field and follows next like any array; growing means a new NativeArray and a copy, with Dispose() on the old one. Inside NativeParallelMultiHashMap from Unity Collections you find the same chains: an array of next indices and an array of buckets.

The doubly linked variant adds a second field, prev: O(1) removal of a known node, like LinkedList<T>, but with no objects. That is the allocation-free LRU cache from the data-structure design unit.
cards/11/q: Reversing a list on indices: next[i] is the index of the next node, −1 is the end. Assemble it following the reference-based reversal.
cards/11/explain: The same reversal as with references: the end is −1, not 0 (0 is the real index of the first cell). First save the next one, nx = next[cur], then reverse the arrow, next[cur] = prev, then move on. Not a single object — an int array can be walked even in Burst.
cards/12/q: You are solving Reverse Nodes in k-Group out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: leave a tail shorter than k alone, change only links, k may be 1 or n
cards/12/items/1: The plan: a dummy, count k nodes, reverse the piece, attach it, move to the next group
cards/12/items/2: Name the pointers: groupPrev, kth, groupNext, first — and what each one means
cards/12/items/3: Reverse the group with prev = groupNext — the group’s tail attaches by itself
cards/12/items/4: Attach: groupPrev.next = kth, then groupPrev = first
cards/12/items/5: Run 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 with k = 2 and show that 5 stays in place
cards/12/items/6: Complexity: O(n) time, each node twice; O(1) memory
cards/12/explain: The problem with its extreme k, the whole plan, then the pointers and their meaning — before the code, so the interviewer can follow them. Then the two attaching steps, a run with a tail shorter than k, and the complexity.
cards/13/q: Match the structure or operation with its cost.
cards/13/pairs/0/1: About 48 bytes and an allocation per insert
cards/13/pairs/2/1: O(n): a walk around the ring
cards/13/pairs/4/0: Remove from List<T> when order does not matter
